title: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
summary: CNNs are specialized networks for images. Convolution layers detect local patterns (edges, textures) that combine into complex features. Understanding CNNs matters for GenAI because image-generation models like diffusion models build on convolutional
content:
# Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) ##### 1,200 images and two very different results An agritech startup in Nashik needed to classify grape leaf diseases from phone photos. Their field team collected 1,200 labelled images across four classes — downy mildew, powdery mildew, anthracnose, and healthy. Attempt one: a CNN built from scratch. Four convolutional blocks, trained for 60 epochs. Validation accuracy peaked at **58%**, with training accuracy at 97%. Textbook overfitting on a small dataset. Attempt two, the following week: they downloaded ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet, froze everything except the final layer, and replaced that layer with a 4-class output. Training took eleven minutes on a laptop GPU. Validation accuracy: **89%**. Then they unfroze the last convolutional block and fine-tuned at a low learning rate for ten more epochs. **93.5%.** Same data. Same architecture family. The difference is that ResNet-50 had already spent weeks learning what edges, textures, curves, and colour gradients look like, from 1.2 million ImageNet photographs. Grape leaves were not in ImageNet — but *leaf-shaped things with blotchy textures* are made of exactly the visual primitives ImageNet teaches. **Transfer learning is the single most valuable practical technique in computer vision**, and understanding why requires understanding what a convolution actually does. That is where we start. ##### Why not just use a dense network? Take a modest 224×224 colour image. Flattened, that is 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 numbers. Connect it to a single hidden layer of 1,000 neurons and you need **150 million weights** — for one layer. Worse, a dense layer treats every pixel as unrelated to its neighbours. It has no notion that pixel (100, 100) is next to pixel (100, 101). And if you train it to recognise a cat in the top-left corner, it learns nothing about cats in the bottom-right. Convolutions fix all three problems with two ideas: - **Local connectivity** — each neuron looks at a small patch, not the whole image. Vision is local; an edge is defined by a few adjacent pixels. - **Weight sharing** — the same small filter slides across the entire image. Learn "vertical edge detector" once and apply it everywhere. This is *translation invariance*, and it is why a CNN recognises a cat regardless of position. ##### Convolution layers A convolution slides a small grid of weights (a **kernel** or **filter**, typically 3×3) across the image, computing a dot product at each position. ``` Input patch Kernel (vertical edge) Output ┌───┬───┬───┐ ┌────┬───┬────┐ │ 10│ 10│200│ │ -1 │ 0 │ +1 │ ├───┼───┼───┤ ⊗ ├────┼───┼────┤ = (10·-1 + 200·1) × 2 │ 10│ 10│200│ │ -2 │ 0 │ +2 │ + (10·-2 + 200·2) ├───┼───┼───┤ ├────┼───┼────┤ = 760 → strong response │ 10│ 10│200│ │ -1 │ 0 │ +1 │ └───┴───┴───┘ └────┴───┴────┘ ``` That kernel responds strongly where dark meets light horizontally — a vertical edge. **The crucial point: in a CNN you do not design these kernels. The network learns them by gradient descent.** The famous result is that the first layer of almost any trained CNN learns edge and colour-blob detectors that look remarkably like the ones neuroscientists found in the mammalian visual cortex. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn conv = nn.Conv2d( in_channels=3, # RGB input out_channels=32, # learn 32 different filters kernel_size=3, stride=1, # step size as the filter slides padding=1, # 'same' padding: output keeps input's H,W ) x = torch.randn(8, 3, 224, 224) # (batch, channels, height, width) out = conv(x) print(out.shape) # torch.Size([8, 32, 224, 224]) print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in conv.parameters())) # 3*3*3*32 + 32 = 896 ← versus 150 million for a dense layer ``` **896 parameters.** That is the efficiency of weight sharing. The output size formula, worth knowing because shape errors are constant in CNN work: $$H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor \frac{H_{\text{in}} + 2p - k}{s} \right\rfloor + 1$$ With `kernel_size=3, padding=1, stride=1`, the output matches the input size — the standard "same" configuration. ##### Feature maps and hierarchy Each of those 32 output channels is a **feature map**: a spatial grid showing where that filter responded strongly. Stack convolutions and the features become progressively more abstract. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Input image
224×224×3"] --> B["Conv block 1
112×112×64"] B --> C["Conv block 2
56×56×128"] C --> D["Conv block 3
28×28×256"] D --> E["Conv block 4
14×14×512"] E --> F["Global pooling
1×1×512"] F --> G["Dense → classes"] B -.detects.-> B1["edges, colour blobs"] C -.detects.-> C1["corners, textures, curves"] D -.detects.-> D1["patterns, object parts"] E -.detects.-> E1["whole objects, semantics"] ``` Notice the trade: **spatial size shrinks, channel count grows.** The network gives up "where exactly" in exchange for "what, in richer detail." This hierarchy is precisely why transfer learning works. The Nashik team's grape leaves needed layers 1–3 (edges, textures, blotch patterns) essentially unchanged from ImageNet. Only the final classification needed to be new. ##### Pooling layers Pooling downsamples a feature map, reducing computation and adding a little robustness to small shifts. ```python nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2) # take the max of each 2×2 patch nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2) # take the mean nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1)) # collapse to 1×1 whatever the input size ``` Max pooling keeps the strongest activation in each patch — "was this feature present anywhere here?" — and halves the height and width. `AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1,1))` is **global average pooling**, and it is what modern architectures use before the classifier. It averages each channel to a single number, so the head does not care about input resolution and you avoid an enormous flatten-to-dense layer. It is a major reason ResNet has 25 million parameters while VGG-16 has 138 million. ##### A CNN from scratch ```python import torch.nn as nn class SmallCNN(nn.Module): """CIFAR-10 style CNN: 32×32×3 input, 10 classes.""" def __init__(self, num_classes=10): super().__init__() def block(cin, cout): return nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(cin, cout, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(cout), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(cout, cout, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(cout), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(2), ) self.features = nn.Sequential( block(3, 64), # 32 -> 16 block(64, 128), # 16 -> 8 block(128, 256), # 8 -> 4 ) self.pool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1) self.classifier = nn.Sequential( nn.Flatten(), nn.Dropout(0.4), nn.Linear(256, num_classes), ) def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) x = self.pool(x) return self.classifier(x) model = SmallCNN() print("parameters:", f"{sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,}") # ~1.2M ``` The `Conv → BatchNorm → ReLU` block is the standard unit. `bias=False` on the conv is deliberate — BatchNorm has its own shift parameter, so the conv bias is redundant. ##### Data augmentation With 1,200 images you will overfit. Augmentation manufactures variety by applying random label-preserving transformations, so the model sees a slightly different image every epoch. ```python from torchvision import transforms IMAGENET_MEAN = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] IMAGENET_STD = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225] train_tf = transforms.Compose([ transforms.RandomResizedCrop(224, scale=(0.7, 1.0)), transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5), transforms.RandomRotation(degrees=15), transforms.ColorJitter(brightness=0.25, contrast=0.25, saturation=0.25), transforms.ToTensor(), transforms.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD), transforms.RandomErasing(p=0.25), ]) eval_tf = transforms.Compose([ # NO augmentation at eval time transforms.Resize(256), transforms.CenterCrop(224), transforms.ToTensor(), transforms.Normalize(IMAGENET_MEAN, IMAGENET_STD), ]) ``` **Augmentation must preserve the label.** A horizontal flip of a grape leaf is still that disease — fine. A horizontal flip of the digit "2" is not a "2", so `RandomHorizontalFlip` is wrong for MNIST. And for the Nashik case, aggressive `ColorJitter` would be actively harmful, because disease diagnosis depends heavily on colour. Think about what varies in the real world and augment along *those* axes: field photos vary in lighting, angle, and distance, so crops, rotations, and mild brightness changes are the right choices. **Never augment validation or test data.** You need a stable, comparable evaluation. Those specific `IMAGENET_MEAN`/`STD` numbers matter for transfer learning: a pretrained model expects inputs normalised the same way its training data was. ##### CNN architectures | Architecture | Year | Key idea | Params | |---|---|---|---| | **LeNet-5** | 1998 | First practical CNN, digit recognition | 60K | | **AlexNet** | 2012 | ReLU, dropout, GPUs; won ImageNet by 10 points | 60M | | **VGG-16** | 2014 | Depth via stacked 3×3 convs | 138M | | **ResNet-50** | 2015 | Skip connections enabled 100+ layers | 25M | | **EfficientNet** | 2019 | Balanced scaling of depth/width/resolution | 5–66M | | **ConvNeXt** | 2022 | CNN modernised with transformer-era design | 29–198M | AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) is the one that started the deep learning boom — it cut ImageNet error from 26% to 15% and made it undeniable that deep nets worked. ResNet's contribution is the **residual connection**: `output = F(x) + x`. That addition gives gradients a direct path backwards, bypassing the multiplication chain from Day 14. It is the same trick transformers use, and it is why 152-layer networks became trainable. **ResNet-50 remains the sensible default** for transfer learning: well-understood, widely available, strong accuracy, reasonable size. ##### Transfer learning The technique that turned 58% into 93.5%. ```python import torch, torch.nn as nn from torchvision import models device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") # 1. Load pretrained weights model = models.resnet50(weights=models.ResNet50_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V2) # 2. Freeze the backbone — it already knows edges, textures, shapes for param in model.parameters(): param.requires_grad = False # 3. Replace the classifier head with one for YOUR classes num_features = model.fc.in_features # 2048 for ResNet-50 model.fc = nn.Sequential( nn.Dropout(0.3), nn.Linear(num_features, 4), # 4 grape diseases ) model = model.to(device) trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad) print(f"training {trainable:,} of {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,}") # training 8,196 of 23,516,228 # 4. Stage one: train the head only optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.fc.parameters(), lr=1e-3) criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1) # ... run ~10 epochs ... # 5. Stage two: unfreeze the last block and fine-tune at a LOW lr for param in model.layer4.parameters(): param.requires_grad = True optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([ {"params": model.layer4.parameters(), "lr": 1e-5}, # gentle on pretrained weights {"params": model.fc.parameters(), "lr": 1e-4}, ], weight_decay=1e-4) # ... run ~10 more epochs ... ``` **The two-stage recipe is what makes this work.** If you unfreeze everything immediately, the large random gradients from the untrained head flow backwards and destroy the carefully learned features before they can help — a phenomenon called catastrophic forgetting. Train the head first so its gradients are sensible, *then* unfreeze gently. **How much to unfreeze**, by dataset size: | Your data | Strategy | |---|---| | < 1,000 images | Freeze everything; train the head only | | 1,000–10,000 | Freeze most; fine-tune the last block or two | | 10,000–100,000 | Fine-tune the whole network at a low LR | | > 100,000, very different domain | Consider training from scratch | And a rule of thumb for the learning rate: **fine-tuning uses 10–100× lower LR than training from scratch.** ##### Common mistakes - **Training from scratch on a small dataset** when transfer learning would work far better — the 58% versus 93.5% gap. - **Unfreezing everything at once**, destroying pretrained features. - **Using the same learning rate for pretrained backbone and new head.** - **Wrong normalisation statistics** for a pretrained model. Use ImageNet's mean and std. - **Augmenting the validation or test set.** - **Label-breaking augmentation** — horizontal flips on digits or text, heavy colour jitter on colour-dependent tasks. - **Forgetting the channel order.** PyTorch is (B, C, H, W); TensorFlow is (B, H, W, C). - **A giant flatten-to-dense layer** instead of global average pooling. - **No BatchNorm**, making a deep CNN slow and unstable to train. - **Forgetting `model.eval()`**, so BatchNorm uses batch statistics at inference. - **Batch size too large for your GPU** — reduce it or use gradient accumulation. - **Assuming more augmentation is always better.** Too aggressive and the model cannot learn the actual signal. ##### Hands-on: measure the gap yourself Your practical task is a CNN on CIFAR-10 in PyTorch or Keras. Use the `SmallCNN` structure above as a starting point and add basic augmentation (random crop with padding 4, plus horizontal flip — the standard CIFAR recipe). Expect roughly 85–90% after 30 epochs. Print `model.summary()` or the parameter count and check the shape after each block; CIFAR's 32×32 input means you can only pool about three times before running out of spatial dimensions. The mini project uses transfer learning with a pretrained ResNet on your own images. Collect them yourself — 40 photos each of five things around you is enough, and using your own data makes the result far more satisfying than another benchmark. Follow the two-stage recipe and log validation accuracy after each stage separately, so you can see what freezing bought and what fine-tuning added. The assignment compares from-scratch against transfer learning on the same dataset. Report three things: final accuracy, epochs to reach 80% of final accuracy, and total training time. The pattern you will see — pretrained reaching in three epochs what scratch takes forty to approach, if it gets there at all — is worth writing up carefully. Then explain *why* using the feature hierarchy: the pretrained model did not need to relearn what an edge is. ##### Key takeaways - **Convolutions exploit locality and weight sharing**, cutting a 150-million-parameter dense layer to 896 while gaining translation invariance. - **CNNs build a hierarchy** — edges, then textures, then parts, then objects — with spatial size shrinking as channel depth grows. - **Transfer learning is the highest-leverage technique in vision.** Reuse a pretrained backbone, replace the head, and beat a from-scratch model by 30+ points on small datasets. - **Fine-tune in two stages**: train the new head with the backbone frozen, then unfreeze the last block at a 10–100× lower learning rate. - **Augment training data only**, choose transformations that preserve the label and mirror real-world variation, and use ImageNet normalisation with pretrained models.
practical_task_reference: Build a CNN in PyTorch or Keras to classify CIFAR-10 images and report accuracy.
mini_project_reference: Use transfer learning with a pretrained ResNet to classify a custom set of images with high accuracy.
